outnoise: To exceed in noise; to surpass in noisiness. Fuller.
outline: 1. (a) The line which marks the outer limits of an object or figure; the exterior line or edge; contour. (b) In art: A line drawn by pencil, pen, graver, or the like, by which the boundary of a… | 1. To draw the outline of. 2. Fig.: To sketch out or indicate as by an outline; as, to outline an argument or a campaign.
outbuild: To exceed in building, or in durability of building.
outskirt: A part remote from the center; outer edge; border; -- usually in the plural; as, the outskirts of a town. Wordsworth. The outskirts of his march of mystery. Keble.
outsell: 1. To exceed in amount of sales; to sell more than. 2. To exceed in the price of selling; to fetch more than; to exceed in value. Fuller. Shak.
outlier: 1. One who does not live where his office, or business, or estate, is. Bentley. 2. That which lies, or is, away from the main body. 3. (Geol.) A part of a rock or stratum lying without, or beyond, the main body, from which it has been separated by denudation.
outgrow: 1. To surpass in growing; to grow more than. Shak. 2. To grow out of or away from; to grow too large, or too aged, for; as, to outgrow clothing; to outgrow usefulness; to outgrow an infirmity.
outness: 1. The state of being out or beyond; separateness. 2. (Metaph.) The state or quality of being distanguishable from the perceiving mind, by being in space, and possessing marerial quality; externality; objectivity. The outness of the objects of sense. Sir W. Hamiltom.
outright: 1. Immediately; without delay; at once; as, he was killed outright. 2. Completely; utterly. Cardinal Manning.
outgoer: One who goes out or departs.
outshine: To shine forth. "Bright, outshining beams." Shak. | To excel in splendor. A throne of royal state, which far Outshone the wealth of Ormus and of Ind. Milton.
outwing: To surpass, exceed, or outstrip in flying. Garth.
outpace: To outgo; to move faster than; to leave behind. Lamb.
outbabble: To utter foolishly or excessively; to surpass in babbling. Milton.
outluster: To excel in brightness or luster. Shak.
outlook: 1. To face down; to outstare. To outlook conquest, and to win renown. Shak. 2. To inspect throughly; to select. (old) Cotton. | 1. The act of looking out; watch. 2. One who looks out; also, the place from which one looks out; a watchower. Lyon Playfair. 3. The view obtained by one looking out; scope of vision; prospect;
outfitter: One who furnishes outfits for a voyage, a journey, or a business.
outcry: 1. A vehement or loud cry; a cry of distress, alarm, opposition, or detestation; clamor. 2. Sale at public auction. Massinger. Thackeray.
oust: 1. To take away; to remove. Multiplication of actions upon the case were rare, formerly, and thereby wager of law ousted. Sir M. Hale. 2. To eject; to turn out. Blackstone. From mine own earldom foully ousted me. Tennyson.
outguard: A guard or small body of troops at a distance from the main body of an army, to watch for the approach of an enemy; hence, anything for defense placed at a distance from the thing to be defended.
ouster: A putting out of possession; dispossession; ejection; disseizin. Ouster of the freehold is effected by abatement, intrusion, disseizin, discontinuance, or deforcement. Blackstone. Ouster le main. Etym: [Ouster + F. la main the hand, L. manus.] (Law) A delivery of lands out of the hands of a guardian, or out of the king's hands, or a judgement given for that purpose. Blackstone.
outkeeper: An attachment to a surveyor's compass for keeping tally in chaining.
outport: A harbor or port at some distance from the chief town or seat of trade. Macaulay.
outname: 1. To exceed in naming or describing. 2. To exceed in name, fame, or degree. (old) And found out one to outname thy other faults. Beau. & Fl.
ouananiche: A small landlocked variety of the Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar ounaniche) of Lake St. John, Canada, and neighboring waters, noted for its vigor and activity, and habit of leaping from the water when hooked.
outwell: To pour out. (old) Spenser. | To issue forth. Thomson.
outpass: To pass beyond; to exceed in progress.
outsit: To remain sitting, or in session, longer than, or beyond the time of; to outstay.
outer: Being on the outside; external; farthest or farther from the interior, from a given station, or from any space or position regarded as a center or starting place; -- opposed to inner; | (a) The part of a target which is beyond the circles surrounding the bull's-eye. (b) A shot which strikes the outer of a target.
outhaul: A rope used for hauling out a sail upon a spar; -- opposite of inhaul.
outstrip: To go faster than; to outrun; to advance beyond; to leave behing. Appetites which . . . had outstripped the hours. Southey. He still outstript me in the race. Tennyson.
outlearn: 1. To excel or surpass in learing. 2. To learn out [i. e., completely, utterly]; to exhaust knowledge of. Naught, according to his mind, He could outlearn. Spenser. Men and gods have not outlearned it [love]. Emerson.
outdream: To pass, or escape, while dreaming. "To oultdream dangers." Beau. & Fl.
outstand: To stand out, or project, from a surface or mass; hence, to remain standing out. | 1. To resist effectually; to withstand; to sustain without yielding. Woodward. 2. To stay beyond. "I have outstood my time." Shak.
outgush: A pouring out; an outburst. A passionate outgush of emotion. Thackeray.
outscout: To overpower by disdain; to outface. (old) Marston.
outrode: An excursion. (old) "Outrodes by the ways of Judea." Macc. xv. 41 (Geneva Bible).
outdoors: Abread; out of the house; out of doors.
outerly: 1. Utterly; entirely. (old) Chaucer. 2. Toward the outside. Grew.
outfrown: To frown down; to overbear by frowning. Shak.
outstay: To stay beyond or longer than. She concluded to outstay him. Mad. D' Arblay.
outdoor: Being, or done, in the open air; being or done outside of certain buildings, as poorhouses, hospitals, etc.; as, outdoor exercise; outdoor relief; outdoor patients.
outcome: That which comes out of, or follows from, something else; issue; result; consequence; upshot. "The logical outcome." H. Spenser. All true literature, all genuine poetry, is the direct outcome, the condensed essence, of actual life and thougth. J. C. Shairp.
outbid: To exceed or surpass in bidding. Prevent the greedy, and outbid the bold. Pope.
ousel: One of several species of European thrushes, especially the blackbird (Merula merula, or Turdus merula), and the mountain or ring ousel (Turdus torquatus). [Written also ouzel.] Rock ousel (Zoöl.), the ring ousel. -- Water ousel (Zoöl.), the European dipper (Cinclus aquaticus), and the American dipper (C. Mexicanus).
outbrag: To surpass in bragging; hence, to make appear inferior. Whose bare outbragg'd the web it seemed to wear. Shak.
outdo: To go beyond in performance; to excel; to surpass. An imposture outdoes the original. L' Estrange. I grieve to be outdone by Gay. Swift.
outground: Ground situated at a distance from the house; outlying land.
outparish: A parish lying without the walls of, or in a remote part of, a town. Graunt.
outterm: An external or superficial thing; outward manner; superficial remark, etc. (old) Not to bear cold forms, nor men's outterms. B. Jonson.
outpray: To exceed or excel in prayer.
outwear: 1. To wear out; to consume or destroy by wearing. Milton. 2. To last longer than; to outlast; as, this cloth will outwear the other. "If I the night outwear." Pope.
outclimb: To climb bevond; to surpass in climbing. Davenant.
outmost: Farthest from the middle or interior; farthest outward; outermost.
outwalk: To excel in walking; to leave behind in walking. B. Jonson.
outre: Being out of the common course or limits; extravagant; bizarre.
outrun: To exceed, or leave behind, in running; to run faster than; to outstrip; to go beyond. Your zeal outruns my wishes. Sir W. Scott. The other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulcher. Jhon xx. 4.
outdweller: One who holds land in a parish, but lives elsewhere. [Eng.]
outrunner: An offshoot; a branch. "Some outrunner of the river." Lauson.
outreason: To excel or surpass in reasoning; to reason better than. South.
outwit: To surpass in wisdom, esp. in cunning; to defeat or overreach by superior craft. They did so much outwit and outwealth us ! Gauden. | The faculty of acquiring wesdom by observation and experience, or the wisdom so acquired; -- opposed to inwit. (old) Piers Plowman.
ouzel: Same as Ousel. The mellow ouzel fluted in the elm. Tennyson.
ouarine: A Brazilian monkey of the genus Mycetes.
outstorm: To exceed in storming. Insults the tempest and outstorms the skies. J. Barlow.
outscorn: To confront, or subdue, with greater scorn. Shak.
outherod: To surpass (Herod) in violence or wickedness; to exceed in any vicious or offensive particular. "It out-Herods Herod." Shak. Out-Heroding the preposterous fashions of the times. Sir W. Scott.
outvote: To exceed in the number of votes given; to defeat by votes. South.
outquench: To quench entirely; to extinguish. "The candlelight outquenched." Spenser.
outwin: To win a way out of. (old)
outride: To surpass in speed of riding; to ride beyond or faster than. Shak. | 1. A riding out; an excursion. 2. A place for riding out.
outsail: To excel, or to leave behind, in sailing; to sail faster than. Beau. & Fl.
outgaze: To gaze beyond; to exceed in sharpness or persistence of seeing or of looking; hence, to stare out of countenance.
ouch: A socket or bezel holding a precious stone; hence, a jewel or ornament worn on the person. A precious stone in a rich ouche. Sir T. Elyot. Your brooches, pearls, and ouches. Shak.
outcrop: (a) The coming out of a stratum to the surface of the ground. Lyell. (b) That part of inclined strata which appears at the surface; basset. | To come out to the surface of the ground; -- said of strata.
outbrave: 1. To excel in bravery o 2. To excel in magnificence or comeliness. The basest weed outbraves his dignity. Shak.
outplay: To excel or defeat in a game; to play better than; as, to be outplayed in tennis or ball.
outsettler: One who settles at a distance, or away, from others.
outdare: To surpass in daring; to overcome by courage; to brave. Shak. R. Browning.
outscouring: That which is scoured out o Buckland.
outlinear: Of or pertaining to an outline; being in, or forming, an outline. Trench.
outrage: 1. Injurious violence or wanton wrong done to persons or things; a gross violation of right or decency; excessive abuse; wanton mischief; gross injury. Chaucer. He wrought great outrages, wasting all… | 1. To commit outrage upon; to subject to outrage; to treat with violence or excessive abuse. Base and insolent minds outrage men when they have hope of doing it without a return. Atterbury.
outtaken: or prep. Excepted; save. (old) Wyclif. Chaucer.
outrank: To exceed in rank; hence, to take precedence of.
outbray: 1. To exceed in braying. 2. To emit with great noise. (old) Fairfax.
outlying: Lying or being at a distance from the central part, or the main body; being on, or beyond, the frontier; exterior; remote; detached.
outblush: To exceed in blushing; to surpass in rosy color. T. Shipman.
outreckon: To exceed in reckoning or computation. Bp. Pearson.
outdwell: To dwell or stay beyond. (poetic) "He outdwells his hour." Shak.
outsole: The outside sole of a boot or shoe.
outing: 1. The act of going out; an airing; an excursion; as, a summer outing. 2. A feast given by an apprentice when he is out of his time. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
outspeak: 1. To exceed in speaking. 2. To speak openly or boldly. T. Campbell. 3. To express more than. Shak.
outwards: From the interior part; in a direction from the interior toward the exterior; out; to the outside; beyond; off; away; as, a ship bound outward. The wrong side may be turned outward. Shak. Light falling on them is not reflected outwards. Sir I. Newton. Outward bound, bound in an outward direction or to foreign parts; -- said especially of vessels, and opposed to homeward bound.
outbreast: To surpass in singing. See Breast, n., 6. (old)
outlast: To exceed in duration; to survive; to endure longer than. Milton.
outdated: Being out of date; antiquated. (old) Hammond.
outface: To face or look (one) out of countenance; to resist or bear down by bold looks or effrontery; to brave. Shak. Having outfaced all the world. South.
outfield: 1. Arable land which has been or is being exhausted. See Infield, 1. [Scot.] 2. A field beyond, or separated from, the inclosed land about the homestead; an uninclosed or unexplored tract. Also used figuratively. The great outfield of thought or fact. Trench. 3. (Baseball) The part of the field beyond the diamond, or infield. It is occupied by the fielders. 4.
outofdoor: Being out of the house; being, or done, in the open air; outdoor; as, out-of-door exercise. See Out of door, under Out, adv. Amongst out-of-door delights. G. Eliot.
outspoken: Speaking, or spoken, freely, openly, or boldly; as, an outspoken man; an outspoken rebuke. -- Out*spo"ken*ness, n.
outbrazen: To bear down with a brazen face; to surpass in impudence. T. Brown.
ounding: Waving. (old) Ounding, paling, winding, or bending . . . of cloth. Chaucer.
outbowed: Convex; curved outward. "The convex or outbowed side of a vessel." Bp. Hall.
output: 1. The amount of coal or ore put out from one or more mines, or the quantity of material produced by, or turned out from, one or more furnaces or mills, in a given time. 2. (Physiol.) That which is thrown out as products of the metabolic activity of the body; the egesta other than the fæces. See Income.
ous: 1. An adjective suffix meaning full of, abounding in, having, possessing the qualities of, like; as in gracious, abounding in grace; arduous, full of ardor; bulbous, having bulbs, bulblike; riotous, poisonous, piteous, joyous, etc. 2. (Chem.) A suffix denoting that the element indicated by the name bearing it, has a valence lower than that denoted by the termination -ic;
outpower: To excel in power; to overpover. (old) Fuller.
outhouse: A small house or building at a little distance from the main house; an outbuilding.
outargue: To surpass or conquer in argument.
outlie: To exceed in lying. Bp. Hall.
outprize: To prize beyong value, or in excess; to exceed in value. (old) Shak.
outflank: To go beyond, or be superior to, on the flank; to pass around or turn the flank or flanks of.
outwind: To extricate by winding; to unloose. Spenser. Dr. H. More.
outfoot: To outrun or outwalk; hence, of a vessel, to outsail. [Colloq.]
outcast: Cast out; degraded. "Outcast, rejected." Longfellow. | 1. One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home, society, or country; hence, often, a degraded person; a vagabond. The Lord . . . gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. Ps.
outlawry: 1. The act of outlawing; the putting a man out of the protection of law, or the process by which a man (as an absconding criminal) is deprived of that protection. 2. The state of being an outlaw.
outzany: To exceed in buffoonery. (old) B. Jonson.
outgo: 1. To go beyond; to exceed in swiftness; to surpass; to outdo. 2. To circumvent; to overreach. (old) Denham. | That which goes out, or is paid out; outlay; expenditure; -- the opposite of Ant: income. Lowell.
outcompass: To exceed the compass or limits of. Bacon.
outstanding: That stands out; undischarged; uncollected; not paid; as, outstanding obligations. Revenues . . . as well outstanding as collected. A. Hamilton.
outlet: The place or opening by which anything is let out; a passage out; an exit; a vent. Receiving all, and having no outlet. Fuller.
ourselves: ; sing. Ourself (we; also, alone in the predicate, in the nominative or the objective case. We ourselves might distinctly number in words a great deal further then we usually do. Locke. Safe in ourselves, while on ourselves we stand. Dryden. Note: The form ourself is usec only in the regal or formal style after we or us, denoting a single person.
outboard: Beyond or outside of the lines of a vessel's bulwarks or hull; in a direction from the hull or from the keel; -- opposed to inboard; as, outboard rigging; swing the davits outboard.
outmanoeuvre: To surpass, or get an advantage of, in maneuvering; to outgeneral.
outstart: To start out or up. Chaucer.
outset: A setting out, starting, or beginning. "The outset of a political journey." Burke. Giving a proper direction to this outset of life. J. Hawes.
outdraw: To draw out; to extract. "He must the teeth outdraw." Gower.
oul: An awl. (old) Chaucer. | An owl. (old) Chaucer.
outtongue: To silence by talk, clamor, or noise. Shak.
outthrow: 1. To throw out. Spenser. 2. To excel in throwing, as in ball playing.
outfangthef: (a) A thief from without or abroad, taken within a lord's fee or liberty. (b) The privilege of trying such a thief. Burrill.
outspan: To unyoke or disengage, as oxen from a wagon. [S. Africa]
outfly: To surpass in flying; to fly beyond or faster than. Shak. Winged with fear outflies the wind. Waller.
outpour: A flowing out; a free discharge.
outbreak: A bursting forth; eruption; insurrection. "Mobs and outbreaks." J. H. Newman. The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind. Shak.
outrigger: 1. Any spar or projecting timber run out for temporary use, as from a ship's mast, to hold a rope or a sail extended, or from a building, to support hoisting teckle. 2. (Naut.) (a) A projecting support for a rowlock, extended from the side of a boat. (b) A boat thus equipped.
outswell: 1. To exceed in swelling. 2. To swell beyond; to overflow. (old) Hewyt.
outsee: To see beyond; to excel in cer
outfall: 1. The mouth of a river; the lower end of a water course; the open end of a drain, culvert, etc., where the discharge occurs. 2. A quarrel; a falling out. [Prov. Eng.]
outspend: Outlay; expenditure. A mere outspend of savageness. I. Taylor.
outfit: A fitting out, or equipment, as of a ship for a voyage, or of a person for an expedition in an unoccupied region or residence in a foreign land; things required for equipment; the expense of, or allowance made for, equipment, as by the government of the United States to a diplomatic agent going abroad.
outreign: To go beyond in reigning; to reign through the whole of, or longer than. Spenser.
ought: 1. Was or were under obligation to pay; owed. (old) This due obedience which they ought to the king. Tyndale. The love and duty I long have ought you. Spelman. [He] said . . . you ought him a thousand pound. Shak. 2. Owned; possessed. (old) The knight the which that castle ought. Spenser. 3. To be bound in duty or by moral obligation.
outring: To excel in volume of ringing sound; to ring louder than.
outlive: To live beyond, or longer than; to survive. They live too long who happiness outlive. Dryden.
outgeneral: To exceed in generalship; to gain advantage over by superior military skill or executive ability; to outmaneuver. Chesterfield.
outsport: To exceed in sporting. "Not to outsport discretion." Shak.
outstare: To excel or overcome in staring; to face down. I would outstare the sternest eyes that look. Shak.
outlustre: To excel in brightness or luster. Shak.
outloose: A loosing from; an escape; an outlet; an evasion. (old) That "whereas" gives me an outloose. Selden.
outpost: (a) A post or station without the limits of a camp, or at a distance from the main body of an army, for observation of the enemy. (b) The troops placed at such a station.
outpreach: To surpass in preaching. And for a villain's quick conversion A pillory can outpreach a parson. Trumbull.
outshoot: To exceed or excel in shooting; to shoot beyond. Bacon. Men are resolved never to outshoot their forefathers' mark. Norris.
outrede: To surpass in giving rede, or counsel. (old) See Atrede. Chaucer.
outgoing: 1. The act or the state of going out. The outgoings of the morning and evening. Ps. lxv. 8. 2. That which goes out; outgo; outlay. 3. The extreme limit; the place of ending. | Going out; departing; as, the outgoing administration; an outgoing steamer.
outbuilding: A building separate from, and subordinate to, the main house; an outhouse.
outward: From the interior part; in a direction from the interior toward the exterior; out; to the outside; beyond; off; away; as, a ship bound outward. The wrong side may be turned outward. Shak. | 1. Formmg the superficial part; external; exterior; -- opposed to inward; as, an outward garment or layer. Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. Cor. iv. 16. 2.
outrider: 1. A summoner whose office is to cite men before the sheriff. (old) 2. One who rides out on horseback. (old) Chaucer. 3. A servant on horseback attending a carriage.
ounce: 1. A weight, the sixteenth part of a pound avoirdupois, and containing 437 2. (Troy Weight) The twelfth part of a troy pound. Note: The troy ounce contains twenty pennyweights, each of twenty- four… | A feline quadruped (Felis irbis, or uncia) resembling the leopard in size, and somewhat in color, but it has longer and thicker fur, which forms a short mane on the back.
outstreet: A street remote from the center of a town. Johnson.
outpatient: A patient who is outside a hospital, but receives medical aid from it.
outbreaking: 1. The act of breaking out. 2. That which bursts forth.
outburn: 1. To exceed in burning. 2. To burn entirely; to be consumed. Shak.
outway: A way out; exit. In divers streets and outways multiplied. P. Fletcher.
outwall: The exterior wall; the outside surface, or appearance. Shak.
outwrite: To exceed or excel in writing.
outmarch: To surpass in marching; to march faster than, or so as to leave behind.
outjest: To surpass in jesting; to drive out, or away, by jesting. Shak.
outrush: To rush out; to issue, or ru Garth.
outspread: To spread out; to expand; -- usually as a past part. or adj.
outsider: 1. One not belonging to the concern, institution, party, etc., spoken of; one disconnected in interest or feeling. [Recent] A. Trollope. 2. A locksmith's pinchers for grasping the point of a key in the keyhole, to open a door from the outside when the key is inside. 3. A horse which is not a favorite in the betting. [Cant]
outsentry: A sentry who guards the entrance or approach to a place; an outguard.
oubliette: A dungeon with an opening only at the top, found in some old castles and other strongholds, into which persons condemned to perpetual imprisonment, or to perish secretly, were thrust, or lured to fall. Sudden in the sun An oubliette winks. Where is he Gone. Mrs. Browning.
outleap: To surpass in leaping. | A sally. Locke.
outtravel: To exceed in speed o Mad. D' Arblay.
outgrowth: That which grows out of, or proceeds from, anything; an excrescence; an offshoot; hence, a result or consequence.
out: In its original and strict sense, out means from the interior of something; beyond the limits or boundary of somethings; in a position or relation which is exterior to something; | 1. One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office; -- generally in the plural. 2. A place or space outside of something; a nook or corner; an angle projecting outward;
outmantle: To excel in mantling; hence, to excel in splendor, as of dress. And with poetic trappings grace thy prose, Till it outmantle all the pride of verse. Cowper.
outmeasure: To exceed in measure or extent; to measure more than. Sir T. Browne.
outrageous: Of the nature of an outrage; exceeding the limits of right, reason, or decency; involving or doing an outrage; furious; violent; atrocious. "Outrageous weeping." Chaucer. "The most outrageous villainies." Sir P. Sidney. "The vile, outrageous crimes." Shak. "Outrageous panegyric." Dryden. Syn. -- Violent; furious; exorbitant; excessive; atrocious; monstrous; wanton; nefarious;
outstrike: To strike out; to strike faster than. Shak.
outbalance: To outweight; to exceed in weight or effect. Let dull Ajax bear away my right When all his days outbalance this one night. Dryden.
outjet: That which jets out or projects from anything. H. Miller.
outslide: To slide outward, onward, or forward; to advance by sliding. (poetic) At last our grating keels outslide. Whittier.
outlaw: A person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection. Blackstone. | 1. To deprive of the benefit and protection of law; to declare to be an outlaw; to proscribe. Blackstone. 2. To remove from legal jurisdiction or enforcement; as, to outlaw a debt or claim;
outlay: To lay out; to spread out; to display. Drayton. | 1. A laying out or expending. 2. That which is expended; expenditure. 3. An outlying haunt. (old) Beau. & Fl.
outcrier: One who cries out or proclaims; a herald or crier.
outraye: See Outrage, v. i. (old) This warn I you, that ye not suddenly Out of yourself for no woe should outraye. Chaucer.
outcourt: An outer or exterior court. The skirts and outcourts of heaven. South.
outrance: The utmost or last extremity. Combat à outrance, a fight to the end, or to the death.
outtalk: To overpower by talking; to exceed in talking; to talk down. Shak.
ouphe: A fairy; a goblin; an elf. (old) "Like urchins, ouphes, and fairies." Shak.
outspeed: To excel in speed. Outspeed the realized miracles of steam. Talfourd.
outlimb: , An extreme member or part of a thing; a limb. (old) Fuller.
our: Of or pertaining to us; belonging to us; as, our country; our rights; our troops; our endeavors. See I. The Lord is our defense. Ps. lxxxix. 18. Note: When the noun is not expressed, ours is used in the same way as hers for her, yours for your, etc.; as, whose house is that It is ours. Our wills are ours, we known not how. Tennyson.
outray: To spread out in array. (old) And now they outray to your fleet. Chapman.
outact: To do or beyond; to exceed in acting. He has made me heir to treasures Would make me outact a real window's whining. Otway.
outflow: A flowing out; efflux. | To flow out. Campbell.
outwrest: To extort; to draw from or forth by violence. (old) Spenser.
outbreathe: 1. To breathe forth. "Outbreathed life." Spenser. 2. To cause to be out of breath; to exhaust. Shak. | To issue, as breath; to be breathed out; to exhale. Beau. & Fl.
outparamour: To exceed in the number of mistresses. Shak.
outside: 1. The external part of a thing; the part, end, or side which forms the surface; that which appears, or is manifest; that which is superficial; the exterior. There may be great need of an outside… | 1. Of or pertaining to the outside; external; exterior; superficial. 2. Reaching the extreme or farthest limit, as to extent, quantity, etc.; as, an outside estimate.
outlaugh: 1. To surpass or outdo in laughing. Dryden. 2. To laugh (one) out of a purpose, principle, etc.; to discourage or discomfit by laughing; to laugh down. His apprehensions of being outlaughed will force him to continue in a restless obscurity. Franklin.
outromance: To exceed in romantic character. Fuller.
outtell: To surpass in telling, counting, or reckoning. "I have outtold the clock." Beau. & Fl.
outweigh: To exceed in weight or value.
outermost: Being on the extreme external part; farthest outward; as, the outermost row. Boyle.
outlandish: 1. Foreign; not native. Him did outlandish women cause to sin. Neh. xiii. 26. Its barley water and its outlandish wines. G. W. Cable. 2. Hence: Not according with usage; strange; rude; barbarous; uncouth; clownish; as, an outlandish dress, behavior, or speech. Something outlandish, unearthy, or at variance with ordinary fashion. Hawthorne. --Out*land"ish*ly, adv.
outwork: To exceed in working; to work more or faster than. | A minor defense constructed beyond the main body of a work, as a ravelin, lunette, hornwork, etc. Wilhelm.
outbounds: The farthest or exterior bounds; extreme limits; boundaries. Spenser.
outroad: An excursion. (old) "Outrodes by the ways of Judea." Macc. xv. 41 (Geneva Bible).
outpension: A public pension granted to one not required to live in a charitable institution. -- Out"pen`sion*er, n.
oughtness: The state of being as a thing ought to be; rightness. N. W. Taylor.
outmaneuver: To surpass, or get an advantage of, in maneuvering; to outgeneral.
ourebi: A small, graceful, and swift African antelope, allied to the klipspringer.
ouakari: Any South American monkey of the genus Brachyurus, especially B. ouakari.
